reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Paisley stood at the toy shelf at daycare. She wanted to count the cars all by herself. She pointed at the first car. "One," she said. She pointed at the next one. "Two," she said. Then she stopped. She could not remember what came next. Her mouth made a little frown.

Her friend Mia came over. Mia had crumbs on her chin from snack time. "What comes after two?" Paisley asked her. Mia shook her head. "I forgot too," said Mia.

Then Miss Jo began to sing. Her voice was warm like soup. "One, two, buckle my shoe." Paisley heard the words. The two words at the end sounded alike. Shoe rhymed with two. She saw it, like a joke that made her smile.

"Three, four, shut the door," Miss Jo sang. Paisley ran to the little play door and shut it. The click sounded loud. "Five, six, pick up sticks," Miss Jo sang. Paisley picked up a pencil from the floor. It had a sharp point, so she held it carefully and gave it to Miss Jo.

"Seven, eight, lay them straight," sang Miss Jo. Paisley laid the pencils in a neat row. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen," sang Miss Jo. Mia laughed and flapped her arms like wings.

Then Paisley ran back to the cars. She touched each one. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. All the words came out in a line now. Mia clapped her hands.

"Sing it again," said Mia. So they sang together, all the way to ten.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
story:
Clara went to the community centre with her dad. A big room had small tables and chairs. On one table there were two bowls of crackers.

"Let's count," said Miss Ana. Clara pointed at the crackers. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. The other bowl had three crackers. "That one is more," said Clara, pointing at her bowl. Miss Ana smiled and nodded.

Clara ate one cracker. It was crunchy and good. Then she counted again. "One, two, three, four," she said. She looked at both bowls. Now her bowl had four. The other bowl had three. Her bowl was still more, but only by one.

A boy named Sam came to the table. "Can I have a cracker?" he asked. Clara gave him one from her bowl. Then she counted once more. "One, two, three," she said. Now both bowls had three. "They are the same now," said Clara.

Outside, a car gave a soft ring of its bell. The tall door opened, and more friends came in. Clara waved at Sam. "Do you want to count with me?" she asked. Sam sat down next to her.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Lillian wanted to build a house for her toy snake. She looked for blocks with four sides. She found a square block. It was just right for the door.

Then the block tipped over. Now a corner pointed up. "Oh no!" said Lillian. "That looks like a new shape!" Her brother Tom ran in. "You made a diamond!" he said. Lillian frowned. She needed a square door, not a diamond door.

Lillian turned the block back. The corner went down flat. Tom peeked at it. "Hey, it is still a square!" he said. Lillian laughed. She pushed the square into the wall. The snake slid right in. "Welcome home, silly snake!" said Lillian. Tom clapped his hands. Lillian found a triangle block for the roof. The house was done at last.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Sadie sat in her car seat. She had a bag of crackers. Her dad drove the car. "Big truck!" said Sadie. "Cool truck," said Dad.

Then they stopped. Grandma was in the car too. Grandma looked hungry. Sadie held out her bag. "Crackers? Please take one," said Sadie. Grandma took a cracker. "Thank you, Sadie," said Grandma. Sadie opened her mouth. Then she closed it. What could she say back? She thought and thought. The car went slow. The car went fast.

Then Dad handed Grandma his hat. "Thank you," said Grandma. "You're welcome," said Dad. Sadie sat up tall. Now she knew the words. Grandma took one more cracker. "Thank you, Sadie," said Grandma. "You're welcome," said Sadie. Grandma smiled big. "You're welcome," said Sadie again. Dad read the road sign out loud. "Home soon," he said. Sadie hugged her cracker bag. "You're welcome," she whispered, one more time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Milan ran to his teacher, Miss Ana. "Read the bear story now!" he said.

Miss Ana held up the big book. "The story is not now," she said. "The story is after snack. Now means at this very moment."

Milan sat down at the little table. Now he had a banana. Now he drank his milk. "Is it after snack now?" he asked. "Not yet," said Miss Ana. "Now we wash hands."

Milan washed his hands. He waited on the bright red rug. "Now?" he asked again. Miss Ana smiled. "Now," she said.

Yesterday, Miss Ana had read the duck story. Today it was the bear story. Tomorrow it would be the train story. But now, at this very moment, Milan sat close and listened.

"Once there was a bear," Miss Ana began. Milan clapped his hands. "This is now," he whispered. And he did not miss one single page.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Ibrahim woke up. The sun was in his window. "Time to brush your teeth," said Mama. "We brush in the morning." Ibrahim saw the toothpaste. He squeezed it. It went rip on the brush. He brushed his teeth. They felt clean and good.

Then Ibrahim ate his bread. He drank his milk. One cup, one plate, one sleepy yawn. He played with his blocks. Mama made a warm bath for him. She tested the water with her hand. Ibrahim splashed and laughed. He put on his soft pajamas, one leg, two legs, done.

At last Ibrahim got into bed. He pulled the blanket up. Then he popped back out. "My teeth!" he said. "We brush before bed too!" He ran to the sink. Rip went the paste again. He brushed up and down. Then he ran back to bed. "Good boy," said Mama. She kissed his head and turned off the light.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Kinsley sat in her car seat. She looked out the window. A red truck went by. Then it was gone. Now there was only the road.

"Mommy, is today the library day?" she asked. Yesterday they had no library. Yesterday was a stay-home day. Mom smiled in the mirror. "Yes, it is today. Today is the day that is happening right now." Kinsley kicked her feet. Now they were in the car. Later they would be at the library. Later was coming, but not yet.

The car stopped at a big door. Mom helped Kinsley climb down. Inside, Kinsley found a book about a bunny. The bunny ate a juicy orange carrot. "Can we read it now?" she asked. "Yes, now," said Mom. They sat on a soft rug and read.

When the book was done, Mom said, "We can come back tomorrow. Tomorrow is the day after this one." Kinsley held the book tight. She put it in her bag all by herself. "Bye, bunny," she said. "See you tomorrow."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Arya went to the library with Mama. She wanted the monkey song book. It was not on the shelf! "Where is it?" Arya asked. The librarian smiled. "Let me help you look."

They found the book on the top of a big cart. Arya sat down with five toy monkeys from the toy box.

She sang, "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed." Then one monkey fell off! She put it under the chair. "Four little monkeys jumping on the bed." Another one fell off. She put that one away too. "Three little monkeys jumping on the bed." Down fell another! "Two little monkeys jumping on the bed." One fell off. "One little monkey jumping on the bed." That monkey fell down too.

"Zero monkeys!" Arya laughed. She lined them all up and counted. "One, two, three, four, five. All five came back."

On the way home, they counted the steps together. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." At home, Mama gave Arya a salty pretzel. Arya gave each monkey a pretend bite. "You get one too," she said. Then she put all five on the bed and sang the song again.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Aurora went to the dentist for the first time. She held Mama's hand tight. The chair was big. It went up and down on a wheel. "Can I sit in it?" she asked. "Yes, the dentist will let you," said Mama.

A boy named Sam was there too. He was young, like Aurora. He grabbed a toothbrush from the box. "Oops," he said. "That is my brother's blue one. Mine is green." He put the blue one back. He took the green one. Each person uses their own toothbrush. People do not share toothbrushes.

Aurora looked at the box. "Can I use Sam's green one?" she asked. "No, that one is Sam's," said the dentist. She gave Aurora a new one. It was pink. Aurora smiled. She opened her mouth wide. "Ahh," she said. The dentist counted her teeth. "Ten little teeth," he said. "All clean!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Jacob went to the playground with his baby sister. She needed a nap. She wanted to sleep in her little stroller.

Jacob saw big kids run fast. He saw small kids walk slow. The sun felt hot. His juice box felt cold. He took a sip. It was yummy.

Then Milo came by. Milo had a drum. He banged it loud. Boom, boom, boom! The baby woke up. She cried.

"Can you play quiet?" Jacob asked. "Loud and quiet are opposites."

"Opposites?" said Milo. "Like this?" He tapped the drum soft. Tap, tap, tap. The baby closed her eyes. She went back to sleep.

Jacob rode down the slide. "You saved nap time," he said. "That is the best gift ever."

Milo smiled. "My drum is smelly too. Want a sniff?"

Jacob laughed. "No way!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Leah wants to play rocket ship at the playground. But her rocket is not ready yet. It has a wobbly ladder and a sticky wheel.

Leah cleans the sticky wheel with her sleeve. Now the wheel spins fast. Papa holds the wobbly ladder and fixes it tight. "Thank you, Papa," says Leah.

Now the rocket is ready. A boy named Sam wants to fly too. Leah and Sam make a line to climb in. First Leah, then Sam. "We need a countdown," says Sam. "Count down from ten!"

Leah counts, "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Leah jumps up high. Sam jumps up high too. They fly to the moon together.

Sam holds out his hand. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten stars!" he says. Leah looks up and counts them too. She is so happy.

Then Leah counts down again. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one." Sam jumps. "Blast off!" they shout, and run to the swings.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Leah went to the library with her dad. She wanted to find a book about animals. On the shelf she saw cats, dogs and frogs. "Those are all animals," said the librarian, smiling.

Next Leah found the playroom. A boy named Sam was cleaning up. He held up each thing and said its name. "Blocks," said Sam, dropping them in the toy box. "Dolls." Then a big red ball bounced away. Leah ran and patted it like a drum. "Ball!" she said. Sam put it in the box too. "Blocks, dolls and balls are all toys," Sam said. The box was full now.

Then Leah heard a sniffing sound. A little dog poked its nose under the chair. It had an ugly old sweater on, with one ear flipped up. "A dog in the library?" said Leah. "How did you get in?" The dog wagged its tail and licked her hand.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Paisley ran to the block corner. The blocks were warm in the sun. They smelled like dust and soap.

"I want to build a tall tower," said Paisley. "Ten blocks tall."

She put one block on the mat. Then she put two blocks on top. Then she stopped. Her face felt hot. "What comes after two?" she said.

Her friend Milo was there too. "I forget too," he said. "I only get to two."

Miss Kim sat down with them. "Let me sing you a little rhyme," she said. "One, two, buckle my shoe."

Paisley laughed. "That sounds like a joke. A shoe rhymes with two!"

"Sing it with me," said Miss Kim. "Three, four, shut the door."

Paisley sang it too. The words felt bouncy in her mouth. "Five, six, pick up sticks." She picked up a stick-shaped block. "Seven, eight, lay them straight."

"Now you try the end," said Miss Kim.

Paisley sang the last part all by herself. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen!" She clapped her hands.

Then she stacked the blocks. She touched each one as she said the word. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." The tower stood tall and wobbly.

"Your turn, Milo," said Paisley. "Sing the shoe part first. Then the numbers come out easy."

Milo took a big breath. "One, two, buckle my shoe," he sang.

Paisley held the next block out to him.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Grayson woke up and ran to the window. Snow was everywhere! No school today. He clapped his hands. Then he saw something sad. His toy plane was outside on the porch. It sat under all that snow.

Grayson put on his boots. He stepped into the snow. His feet made marks in it. Every step made a shape. Mom came out too. "Look," said Grayson. "My feet make marks in the snow!"

He walked to the porch. His boots went bump, bump on the bumpy wood. He dug and dug. He found his plane! It was cold and wet. Mom dried it with a towel.

Then Grayson looked back. "Mom! My marks go all the way home!" He followed his own marks back to the door. He jumped in each one. The snow came up over his boots. "Warm cocoa time," said Mom. Grayson held his plane and smiled.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
It was Diwali night at Eleanor's house. Grandma set out little clay lamps in a row. "Diyas," said Grandma. Eleanor counted them. "One, two, three, four, five diyas!"

Eleanor wanted them to glow. "Why are they dark?" she asked. "Look," said Grandma. She touched a match to the first diya. A small flame popped up. Then the second diya glowed. Then the third. The dark room turned warm and bright.

Eleanor clapped her hands. The diyas smelled like warm oil. Their light danced on the wall. Papa lit the last two, one and two. "Now all five are shining," said Eleanor. Grandma laughed. "One little flame, one little lamp, one bright night." Eleanor leaned close to look, but she did not touch. She just watched the lights dance.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Paisley walked up to the bookmobile. It was a big blue truck full of books. Her mom held her hand.

"I want that one!" said Paisley. She pointed at a book about a red fox. The cover felt rough when she touched it.

"You can look at it here," said Mom. "But then we have to give it back."

Paisley sat on the little step. She turned the pages. The fox jumped. The fox ran. The fox slept in leaves. Paisley loved the fox book so much.

The library lady smiled. "Do you want to take it home?" she asked.

Paisley stood up fast. "Home? This book can come home with me?"

"Yes," said the lady. "You need a library card. It lets you borrow books and take them home to read."

"I want a card! I want a card!" said Paisley.

The lady typed on her computer. Then she gave Paisley a small card. It had Paisley's own name on it.

Paisley held the card tight. The lady scanned the card. Then she scanned the fox book. Beep! Beep!

"Now the book is yours to borrow," said the lady. "Bring it back when you are done."

Paisley hugged the book. She skipped all the way to the car. At home, she read the fox book three times. Three whole times!

The next morning, Paisley waved her card at breakfast. "Book day again!" she said. "Can we go back to the blue truck?"

"We can walk there after lunch," said Mom.

Paisley put her card in her pocket. She patted it once more. "Good card," she whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Sophie sat in the car. The new baby sat in his little seat. Mom sat in front. Dad drove.

Sophie counted baby things. One blanket. One hat. One tiny sock. The sock had slipped off. The baby cried. Dad could not reach. Sophie reached over. She pulled the sock back on. The baby stopped crying.

The baby fell asleep. Sophie looked out the window. The sky was deep blue. "Mom," she said, "I miss you. Just you and me." Mom turned around. "I miss that too," said Mom. "It is okay to feel left out. Lots of big sisters do." Sophie nodded. "Can we have our time?" she asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Tomorrow, you and me."

At home, Dad gave Sophie a cookie. Mom fed the baby. Then Mom came back. "Sit with me," said Mom. Sophie sat close on the big chair. "Just us," said Mom. Sophie took a big bite of her cookie and smiled.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story: Jasper sat on his bed. He put on his sock. He put on his shoe. He wanted to go to Mila's house now. "Mila now," he said. Mama shook her head. "Not now, Jasper. It is night. We go tomorrow." Jasper was sorry. His face went sad. "But now," he said. "First we sleep," said Mama. "Then it is tomorrow. Then we go." Jasper got one book. Then he got his bear. Then he got his blanket. One, two, three. Mama read the book. Jasper's eyes closed. He slept all night. Then the sun came up. Light sat on his blanket. "Morning!" said Jasper. "It is today!" He ran to find Mama. "The sleeping is done. Now it is tomorrow. Now we go to Mila's house!" Mama laughed. She took his hand. "Yes. Today we go. You keep your shoes on so we are ready." Jasper looked down at his shoes. He had never taken them off.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Madeline went to the park with Dad. She wanted to paint a card for Grandma. She saw red flowers. She saw blue flowers. She saw yellow flowers too. "Grandma loves pink best," said Madeline. But she had no pink paint.

She sat at the little park table. Dad put out the paints. One cup was red. One cup was white. One cup was green. Madeline frowned at the red cup. "No pink," she said.

Then she had an idea. She dipped her brush in the red paint. She put a red dot on the card. She dipped her brush in the white paint. She stirred the red dot around and around. The red dot turned light. It turned soft. It turned pink! "Pink!" said Madeline. "I made pink!"

She painted one pink flower. Then two pink flowers. Then three pink flowers. She painted green stems. She painted a blue sky. She painted a yellow sun.

Then Dad pushed her on the swing. The swing went high. Madeline held the card tight. "Pink flowers for Grandma!" she called. Dad smiled and gave the swing one more little push.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Declan ran to the block shelf at daycare. Yesterday he made a tall tower. Today he wanted to make a bigger one.

But Nia had the blocks now. She was building a long, long road.

"Can I have the blocks?" Declan asked.

"You can play with them later," said Miss Jo.

"Is it later yet?" Declan asked.

"Not yet," said Miss Jo. "Later means some time after now."

Declan sighed. The blocks looked red and shiny. They made a clack, clack sound when Nia stacked them.

He found some paper. He drew his tower. He stuck a sticker on top. The paper tower was different, but he liked it.

A song played. Then the class had a snack. Then Nia yawned and walked away.

"Is it later now?" Declan asked.

"Yes," said Miss Jo. "It is later now."

Declan hugged the blocks to his chest. "Hello, blocks," he said. "I missed you."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Ivy ran to the swing. "Papa, when is Saturday?" she asked. "Saturday is the day we fly your big red kite," said Papa.

"Not soon enough," said Ivy. "Count the days with me," said Papa. He held up his hand. "Today is Sunday. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." His fingers stopped. "Seven days make one week. Saturday is day seven."

Ivy jumped off the swing. She picked up a stick. "One, two, three," she drew lines in the soft dirt. "Four, five, six, seven." Seven little lines lay in the dirt. Each night, one line would go away.

"Can I make the lines go fast?" asked Ivy. Papa laughed. "Time goes on its own. But you can help it feel quick."

So they counted the slide steps. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight!" Then Ivy was careful going down, so she would not spill her juice cup on the way.

Each day, one line went away. Sunday, Monday, Tuesday. On Saturday morning, one last little line was left. Ivy wiped it with her shoe. "Zero!" she said. "Zero days left!"

Papa held the kite up high. The summer wind pulled it. "One, two, three!" said Papa, and he ran. Ivy ran too, in the bright blue sky's light, chasing the wiggly red tail.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Evan ran into Grandpa's house. On the wall hung big letters. A, B, C, all the way to Z. Evan pointed at the big A. "A!" he shouted. "A says ah, like apple!"

Then Evan found a book. He opened it. There was a small, round letter on the page. It looked shy, hiding at the edge of the word. "Grandpa! A new letter!" cried Evan.

Grandpa laughed. "That is the small a. Big A, small a. They are the same letter."

Evan clapped. He ran back to the wall. He pointed at the big A. Then he ran to the book and pointed at the small a. "Same letter! Same letter!"

A feather drifted down from the shelf and landed on the page, right on the small a. Evan picked it up. He held it high.

"Now I know you, small a," he said. "Ah, ah, apple!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Charlotte wanted to paint a rainbow at school. But the paint shelf had only three pots. There was red. There was yellow. There was blue. Charlotte frowned at them.

A boy named Sam stood next to her. He held the pots up. "Red, yellow and blue are called the primary colours," he said.

Charlotte looked at her blank paper. "How can I paint a rainbow with just three?" she asked.

She dipped her brush in red. Then she dipped it in yellow. The paint on the paper turned orange! Charlotte gasped. She tried red and blue. The paint turned purple. Then she mixed blue and yellow. Green!

The teacher helped her open a big fresh page. Charlotte painted her rainbow, stripe by stripe. Outside, a dog began to bark at the sunny window. Charlotte waved her orange brush at it. "Look at my rainbow!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Aubrey sat at the dinner table. She had peas on her plate. She wanted more peas, but she did not know how to ask.

Daddy held up one finger. "You are this many," he said. Aubrey peeked at his finger. Then she held up three little fingers. "I am three!" she said. Daddy clapped. "Yes! You are three."

Mommy said, "Let's count your peas." Aubrey pointed. "One, two, three, four, five." Mommy smiled. "You counted five peas. Now you can have more." Daddy gave her five more peas.

Aubrey counted them all. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten peas! She ate them one by one.

Then Aubrey felt upset. Her cup was empty. "Uh oh," she said. Mommy poured in milk from the big cup. Aubrey took a big sip.

"I am three," said Aubrey. She held up her fingers to the window, where the river shone far away. "Three, like that!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Hudson was three today. His party was at the bowling alley. Mom held his hand at the door.

His friend Milo arrived. Milo looked sad. "I was scared," Milo said. "I thought we would get lost. I did not know where to go."

Hudson had an idea. He pulled a card from his pocket. It was his party invitation. "See," Hudson said. "The invitation says where. It says the bowling alley. It says when, too. It says three o'clock."

Milo smiled big. "The invitation told me everything," Mom said. "And now you are here, safe with us."

The kids took turns rolling the ball. Hudson rolled slowly. The pins fell down. Crash! Everyone clapped.

Then the cake came out. Hudson blew out the candles with Dad right beside him. Milo sat close by his side.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Jackson sat at the kitchen table. He had a big pencil. He wanted to write his name. "I can do it," he said. Mom sat next to him. Jackson held the pencil in his fist. "Try two fingers on top," said Mom. Jackson tried. The pencil felt better now.

Jackson began at the right side of the paper. He made a J. Then an A. Then the pencil ran out of room. No space for the rest! "Oh no," said Jackson. "The letters won't fit." He had to miss some letters out. His name looked wrong. Mom turned the paper around. "Start here," she said. She pointed to the left side. Jackson started at the left. J, A, C, K. The letters went across the page. There was room for all of them! "Jackson!" he read. Then the door opened. It was Dad, home early, with a wet umbrella. "Is that your name?" Dad asked. Jackson held up the paper. "I wrote it all by myself."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Harper sat in a big blue chair at the dentist. She held her gray toy mouse tight. "It will be okay," said Mama.

The dentist came in. "Hello, Harper," she said. Harper looked at her hands. They were blue. "Why are your hands blue?" Harper asked. "Do you have blue skin?"

The dentist smiled. She pinched one blue finger. Then she pulled it off. Underneath was a pink finger. Harper's eyes went wide. It was not skin. It was a glove.

"Can I see?" asked Harper. The dentist showed her. One glove, two gloves, both blue. She put them on again, snap, snap. Now her hands were clean for looking at teeth. Harper let go of her mouse.

"Open wide," said the dentist. Harper opened her mouth. The dentist counted out loud. "One tooth, two teeth, three teeth." She counted all the way to twenty. Then Harper got a small mirror. She looked at her own teeth and smiled.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Ivy sat on the grass by Grandpa Ben's stone. The stone was warm and dry in the sun. Mama set out a picnic blanket. "We eat lunch here," Mama said. "Grandpa Ben liked picnics."

Ivy was hungry. She grabbed a bread roll right away. Mama held up her hand. "Wait," she said. "First we say our blessing." Ivy put the roll down. She did not know the blessing yet. That was her problem.

Mama folded her hands. "One, we thank the sun. Two, we thank the rain. Three, we thank the farmers." Then Mama began to eat. Ivy looked at her roll. She thought about the farmers. They grew the wheat. That was one more thing to thank.

"I want to say it too," said Ivy. She folded her hands. "One, thank you, sun. Two, thank you, rain. Three, thank you, farmers." Then she took a big breath. "Four, thank you, Grandpa Ben." Mama's eyes went shiny and glad. She gave Ivy a big smile.

Ivy bit into her roll. It tasted good and warm. A little breeze moved the grass near the stone. It felt like a hello. Ivy waved back. "Bye, Grandpa Ben," she said. "Same picnic next week?"

story:
Weston ran to the red basket at daycare. Miss Amy said it was time to play. He tipped the basket over. Lots of little cards fell out. "Oh no," said Weston. "They are all mixed up."

Miss Amy knelt down beside him. "We can fix that," she said. "You can make groups." Weston picked up a card. It had a cow on it. Then he found a duck and a sheep. He put them in one pile. "These are all animals," he said. His friend Mia came to help. She made a pile with a ball, a teddy bear and a truck. "Toys," said Mia. Weston found cards with bread, milk and an apple. He put those in a pile too. "Foods," he said.

One card fell under the table. Weston reached for it carefully. It was a sticky triangle-shaped jam toast card. He laughed and put it with the foods. Mia clapped her hands. "Neat piles!" she said.

Miss Amy looked at all three groups. "Animals, toys and foods," she said. "All in their own spots." Weston smiled big. "We sorted everything!" he said. Then he put the basket away.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Claire wanted to make soup for Grandma. Grandma's house had a big porch with pinecones under the tree. Claire picked three pinecones and put them in a red pot. She poured in dry leaves and stirred with a wooden spoon. "Soup is ready," she said. Grandma sat in her chair and smiled.

Claire held the spoon up to her mouth. She was about to take a big bite. Grandma said, "Stop, sweet pea. Pinecones are pretend food." Claire looked at the spoon. "Pretend food is for pretending to eat," said Grandma. Claire nodded. She lifted the spoon near her lips and made a long slurping sound. "Sluuurp," she said. "Mmm, so good." Grandma slurped too. A bird flew down and hopped close, as if it wanted a taste. "No, bird," said Claire. "This is pretend."

Then Grandma sang a little song about soup, and the bird sang back. Claire clapped. It was her last spoonful of the day, but tomorrow she would make pretend tea. She hugged the pot and hugged Grandma too. "More soup tomorrow," said Claire.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Adam sat at the little red table. Miss Kim put out ten cups. "Let's count," she said. "One, two, three." Adam tapped each cup. "Four, five, six, seven." His friend Mia tapped too. "Eight, nine, ten!"

Adam wanted to write ten on his paper. He wrote 1. Then he stopped. "Why does ten need more?" he asked. Miss Kim sat next to him. "Ten is a 1 and a 0," she said. Adam looked hard. He wrote a 1. Then he wrote a 0 next to it. "Ten!" he shouted. Mia clapped.

Outside, a green leaf blew onto the bench. Adam picked it up and put it by Mia's shoe so she could see. Then it was snack time. Miss Kim gave each child a fresh red apple. Adam took one big bite. Juice ran down his chin. He counted his ten cups again. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!"

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Milan went to the park with his dad. He saw a red strawberry in the picnic basket. "Can I eat it?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. Milan held it up. It smelled so sweet. His nose knew that smell right away.

Then Milan had a funny idea. What if he held his nose shut? He pinched his nose with his fingers. He took a big bite. "Yuck!" he said. "It tastes plain now!" The strawberry tasted like nothing much at all. He let go of his nose. He took another bite. The sweet taste came back! "Dad, my nose helps me taste!" he said.

Dad laughed. "How funny," he said. Milan looked at the ducks on the pond. He listened to them quack. He touched the soft grass with his toes. "What a lucky day," said Milan. He ate one more strawberry, nose wide open.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Jasmine ran to the door. She wanted to play at the park. "Wait," said Mom. "The sun is bright today. Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn." Mom put the shiny white cream on Jasmine's arms. Then she rubbed some on Jasmine's neck and cheeks.

Outside, the sun felt warm. The wind blew hard. Jasmine held her hat with both hands. "Why do I need the cream?" she asked. Mom said, "It keeps the sun from hurting your skin." The wind blew her hat again. The wind was too strong. So Jasmine took off the hat. She put it in the bag.

Jasmine slid down the slide. She dug in the sand. At the end of the day, her skin looked fine. No red spots anywhere. "My skin is happy," said Jasmine. She patted her neck and smiled. "Sunscreen, you did a good job." Then she ran to Mom for a big hug.

activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Asher stood at the school gate. His new backpack sat on his back. It was very full. It was very heavy. His legs felt slow.

Asher wanted to run to the door. But the bag pulled him back. He could not walk fast. He looked in the bag. He saw his toy truck. He saw his toy bear. He saw three more toys.

Asher sat on the wall by the gate. He took the toys out, one by one. His dad held them in his hands. The bag got light. The bag got small on Asher's back.

A girl came to the gate. Her bag was big and round. It looked heavy too. She stopped walking. "My bag is too full," she said. Asher smiled. He showed her how to open his bag. She took out her toy farm animals. Her bag got light too.

Then Asher ran to the door. The wind blew the gate shut. It almost hit a small boy. Asher put out his hand. The gate was slippery from the rain. It slid past his hand anyway. The teacher caught it just in time.

"Now we can wave to our dads," said the girl. They turned around. They waved big waves. And Asher walked into school, quick as a hop.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Sophie ran onto the green grass. Her team wore red shirts. Grandpa sat on the gray bench by the field. He waved at her.

The game began. Sophie got the ball. She kicked it hard. The ball rolled and rolled. But it went the wrong way. It went toward her own net. The other kids ran after it.

"Uh oh," said Sophie. "Which net is mine?" She looked and looked. The red team was at the far end. "That one," she said. She turned around.

She ran fast. Her friend Ben stopped the ball. He passed it to her. Sophie kicked with her foot. The ball went into the other net. The red team cheered.

"Sophie scored!" said Ben. Grandpa clapped and clapped. Sophie smiled a big smile. She did not cry. She hugged the ball.

"Good kick," said Grandpa.

"Again!" said Sophie. And she ran back to the game.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Zoe sat at the paint table at school. She wanted to paint a magic dragon with red, blue and yellow wings. Teacher Maya gave her a brush.

Zoe painted the first wing red. Then she wanted a yellow wing. She put her brush in the yellow paint. But the yellow came out muddy and brown. "Oh no," said Zoe. "My yellow is all dark."

Zoe looked at her cup of water. She rinsed her brush in the water. She wiped it on a leaf-shaped paper towel. Then she put the brush in the yellow paint. This time the yellow was bright like the sun.

Zoe painted the yellow wing. Then she rinsed her brush again. She painted a blue wing too. A polite boy named Sam leaned over. "Your dragon looks like it's glowing," he said.

Zoe tapped the wet yellow wing with her clean blue brush. The two colours hugged and turned green. "A green spark," said Zoe. The dragon had a magic tail now.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Zoey sat at the dinner table. Her little brother Ben sat next to her. Ben had a bumpy toy car with him. He pushed it across his plate.

Then the car fell on the floor. It broke into two pieces. Ben's face turned red. "My car!" he yelled. He was angry. Then his eyes got wet. Big tears ran down his cheeks.

Zoey felt sad too. She remembered her friend at daycare. Her friend cried when she felt sad. Zoey had given her a hug, and her friend smiled.

Zoey climbed down from her chair. She picked up the two pieces. "Father can fix it," she said. Their father got the glue. He glued the car back together. Ben chased the car around the table. He laughed and laughed.

"I happy now!" Ben said. Zoey smiled too.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Edouard stood in the music room. Miss Rosa played a song on the piano. "Now we clap!" she said. Everyone clapped fast. Everyone clapped slow. Edouard clapped too fast. He clapped when the song was quiet. He clapped when the song was loud. His hands went everywhere!

"Can I learn a short song?" Edouard asked. "One that is not long?" Miss Rosa smiled. "Yes! A nursery rhyme is short. It has rhyming words. My grandpa taught me one when I was little." She sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Edouard listened. The words rhymed. Star and are. High and sky.

"Now clap the steady beat," said Miss Rosa. Clap, clap, clap. Edouard clapped with the beat. He sang the rhyme from memory. His hands felt the beat. His mouth sang the words. "I did it!" he laughed. His friend Ben clapped too. They sang the short song two times. Then three times! "Again!" said Edouard.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Sophie ran onto the green grass. Her soccer team was at the park today. Grandpa sat on a gray bench to watch.

"Can we play now?" Sophie asked the coach.

The coach shook her head. "First we warm up," she said. "We run, and we stretch." The whole team ran around in a big circle. Then they touched their toes. Sophie stretched her arms up high.

One boy did not want to warm up. He sat in the grass and began to cry. "I want to kick the ball now," he said. Sophie took his hand. "Come run with me," she said. "Then we can play."

The boy wiped his eyes. He got up and ran with Sophie. He stretched tall like a tree. Then the coach blew her whistle. It was time to play!

Sophie kicked the ball. She ran fast. Her legs felt good and ready. The boy ran fast too. Grandpa waved from the gray bench.

"Did you see my kick?" Sophie called to him.

"I did!" said Grandpa. "Run again!"

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Weston ran to the dress-up corner at daycare. He wanted to wear the firefighter hat. But the big basket was all mixed up.

"A jumble," said Miss Dana. She sat down next to him. "Let's look inside."

Weston dug in. He found a sock. He held it up. "A sock! Socks are not toys. Socks are clothes." He dropped it into the clothes pile. Then he found a bear. "A bear is a toy." He put the bear in the toy bin. He laughed at the silly sock sitting with the bear.

Next he found a shirt. Clothes. A banana from the play kitchen. That was food. He made a food pile too. Soon the basket was empty.

"Where is my hat?" asked Weston. Miss Dana pointed. The hat was on the shelf, next to a triangle block. Weston grabbed it. He put it on his head.

The phone rang, ding ding. It was Baby Sam, crying. His hands were sticky from jam. Weston ran over with a cloth. "I help you," he said. He wiped Sam's hands.

Sam smiled. Weston smiled too. Then he set the phone on the table and put a plate of pretend bananas next to it. "Snack time," he said.
